subChunks.title: Streaming Replication and Read Replicas
subChunks.hookHtml: One database server is a single point of failure and a read bottleneck. Replication adds copies — providing high availability, disaster recovery, and horizontal read scaling.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Streaming replication (PostgreSQL)

PostgreSQL's built-in replication works by shipping WAL (Write-Ahead Log) records from the primary to one or more standby servers. Standbys replay the WAL and stay in sync.

-- On primary: configure pg_hba.conf and postgresql.conf
wal_level = replica
max_wal_senders = 5

-- On standby: set primary_conninfo
primary_conninfo = 'host=primary-db port=5432 user=replicator'

-- Standbys are by default in recovery mode (read-only)

Synchronous vs asynchronous replication

  • Async (default) — the primary commits immediately; the standby catches up shortly after. RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is seconds. Risk: a crash before the standby catches up means small data loss.
  • Sync — the primary waits for at least one standby to acknowledge the WAL before committing. RPO = 0. Cost: higher write latency (must wait for round-trip to standby).
synchronous_commit = on  -- waits for sync standbys
synchronous_standby_names = 'standby1'

Read replicas

Read replicas are hot standbys that accept read queries. Route SELECT queries to replicas; route writes to primary only. This distributes read load horizontally.

Replication lag: a standby may be seconds behind the primary. Read-your-own-writes consistency requires routing a user's reads to the primary (or the same replica) immediately after a write.

Failover

If the primary fails, promote a standby to primary. Tools: pg_auto_failover, Patroni, Repmgr. Managed services (RDS, Cloud SQL, Neon) handle failover automatically.

Logical replication

Streaming replication copies the full WAL. Logical replication copies specific tables or changes, enabling selective replication, cross-version upgrades, and change data capture (CDC).

storyBeats.text: The Academy's single database server handles 50,000 reads per second. It is also the only copy — one disk failure and everything is gone.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Replication serves two purposes: availability and scale. Standbys take over if the primary fails. Read replicas absorb read traffic the primary cannot handle alone. Async replication is fast but risks seconds of data loss. Sync replication is safe but adds latency to every write. Choose by your RPO.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Replication design

Design the replication topology for a system with these requirements: (1) zero data loss on primary failure, (2) 10× read throughput of a single server, (3) the application can tolerate reads being up to 5 seconds stale. How many servers, what type of replication, and how would you route traffic?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Topology: 1 primary + 1 synchronous standby + N async read replicas (e.g. N=3 for 10x reads).

For zero data loss:
- Configure 1 synchronous standby: synchronous_standby_names = 'standby1'
- The primary waits for standby1 to confirm WAL before each commit
- If primary fails, promote standby1 — RPO = 0 (no committed data lost)

For 10× read throughput:
- 3 async read replicas
- Load balancer (PgBouncer or application-level) routes SELECT to replicas round-robin
- Route all writes + read-your-own-write reads to primary

For 5-second staleness tolerance:
- Async replicas lag typically < 1 second under normal load — 5-second tolerance is comfortable
- Monitor max replication lag with SELECT * FROM pg_stat_replication

Final topology:
- primary (writes + sync standby1)
- standby1 (sync — zero RPO, failover candidate)
- replica2, replica3, replica4 (async read replicas — load balanced reads)
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Explain the read-your-own-writes consistency problem in replicated databases and describe two approaches to solve it.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Problem: User writes a post, then immediately reads their post list. Their write went to the primary; their read is routed to a replica. The replica has not yet received the replication event (lag). The user sees their post missing — inconsistent with their own recent action.

Approach 1: Sticky routing — route all reads from a user to the primary for N seconds after they write. After the replica is guaranteed to have caught up (based on observed lag), resume routing reads to replicas. Simple but adds load to primary.

Approach 2: Track replication position — after a write, note the WAL LSN (Log Sequence Number). Route subsequent reads to replicas but check if the replica's applied LSN >= the write's LSN before executing. If the replica is behind, wait briefly or fall back to primary. More precise but requires application support.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between synchronous and asynchronous replication. What does RPO mean and how does replication type affect it?

questions.prompt: What does WAL stand for and what role does it play in replication?
options: Write-Ahead Log — a sequential record of all database changes that standbys replay to stay in sync with the primary
Write and Lock — the mechanism for transaction locking
Wide Area Latency — the network delay between primary and standby
Write Accumulation Layer — a buffer for batch writes
questions.answer: Write-Ahead Log — a sequential record of all database changes that standbys replay to stay in sync with the primary
questions.explanation: WAL (Write-Ahead Log) records every change before applying it to data files. Streaming replication ships WAL records to standbys, which replay them to maintain an identical copy.

questions.prompt: Synchronous replication's main trade-off compared to async is:
options: Higher write latency — the primary waits for standby acknowledgement before committing; in exchange, RPO = 0
Standbys cannot be promoted to primary
Synchronous replication requires more disk space
questions.answer: Higher write latency — the primary waits for standby acknowledgement before committing; in exchange, RPO = 0
questions.explanation: Sync replication adds at least one network round-trip to every commit — the primary cannot acknowledge the client until the standby has confirmed receipt. The benefit is zero data loss on primary failure.

options: The delay between a write being committed on the primary and it being applied on the standby
The time for a standby to start replicating after being created
The overhead that replication adds to primary write performance
The time to complete a failover
questions.answer: The delay between a write being committed on the primary and it being applied on the standby
questions.explanation: Replication lag is the time difference between a commit on the primary and that commit being visible on the standby. Under normal load it is milliseconds. Under high write throughput or network issues it can grow to seconds or more.

questions.prompt: A user updates their profile and immediately loads their profile page. Their read is routed to a replica 2 seconds behind. They see the old profile. What architecture pattern solves this?
options: Read-your-own-writes: route reads to the primary (or track WAL position) for a short window after a write by that user
Use eventual consistency and accept the stale read
Route all reads to the primary permanently
questions.answer: Read-your-own-writes: route reads to the primary (or track WAL position) for a short window after a write by that user
questions.explanation: Read-your-own-writes is a specific consistency guarantee: a user always sees their own writes. Route writes to the primary; route subsequent reads from the same user to the primary (or check WAL LSN) until the replica catches up. Routing all reads to primary defeats the purpose of read replicas.
